title: No Other Good News
sum: Paul opens a letter unlike any of his others. He gives no thanks for his readers. After a greeting that stresses that his authority comes from Jesus Christ and God the Father, not from people (1:1-5), he says he is amazed that the Galatians are switching to a 'different good news', and he curses anyone, even an angel, who preaches another (1:6-10). There is only one good news, and it is the one he told them.

Then Paul tells his own story, to show where his good news came from. He once persecuted the church in his zeal for the traditions of his fathers; God, who had set him apart from his mother's womb, revealed his Son in him; and he went to Arabia, to Damascus, and, three years later, to Jerusalem for only fifteen days with Cephas and James (1:11-24). He did not get his message from the apostles, and the churches of Judea knew him only by report: 'The man who once persecuted us is now telling the good news.'
readings: Read as a defense in court

Hans Dieter Betz read Galatians as a speech for the defense in the ancient manner: opening (1:1-5), statement of facts (1:12-2:14), proposition (2:15-21), proofs (3:1-4:31), advice (5:1-6:10) and conclusion (6:11-18). On this reading chapter 1 answers a charge that Paul's authority was borrowed from Jerusalem and that he had altered his message to please people (1:10).
Read as advice about what to do next

George Kennedy and others argue that the letter is not a defense but a deliberative speech: it aims to move the Galatians to a decision about the future (do not be circumcised). Chapter 1 then sets the stakes: another good news is no good news, and the curse of 1:8-9 shows what is at issue.
Read as the invasion of a new world

J. Louis Martyn reads Galatians as an apocalyptic letter: God has acted in Christ to rescue people from 'the present evil age' (1:4), and Paul's own call was a revelation, not a conversion in the ordinary sense. The question is who rules the world, not merely how an individual is accepted.

views.H: Galatia was a region of central Asia Minor that the Romans had joined in 25 BC to a province reaching south to Pisidia and Lycaonia. Paul's first visit to Jerusalem came after three years (about AD 35-38), and the Nabatean king Aretas IV, who had a governor in Damascus (2 Corinthians 11:32), ruled until about AD 40. The 'regions of Syria and Cilicia' take us to Tarsus and Antioch. Persecution of the church by a zealous Pharisee fits the Jerusalem of the early 30s.
views.C: The letter has no thanksgiving, the one omission that sets it apart from the other letters of Paul; it starts with a rebuke and a curse. Papyrus 46 (about AD 200) preserves the whole letter and Papyrus 51 (5th century) has parts of chapter 1. The scribal changes at 1:3, 1:6, 1:15 and 1:18 are small. Marcion, in the 100s, put Galatians first in his collection of Paul. The letter's authorship is undisputed.
views.L: Chapter 1 is the opening and the first part of a long narrative that runs through 2:14. Three words recur: 'good news' (1:6, 7, 8, 9, 11), 'revelation' (1:12, 16) and 'from' or 'through' (1:1, 11-12). The pattern 'not from people... but through Jesus Christ' (1:1) is repeated in 1:11-12, 1:15-16 and 1:17: Paul's authority and message both come from outside human channels.
views.J: Paul calls his old life 'Judaism' (1:13-14), uses the language of the prophets' calls (Jeremiah 1:5; Isaiah 49:1) and speaks of his mission 'among the Gentiles' (1:16). Stendahl and the 'Paul within Judaism' scholars hear a Jew called to a task, not a convert from one religion to another. James, 'the brother of the Lord' (1:19), is a leading Jewish believer in Jerusalem. The curse of 1:8-9 uses Israel's language of the ban.
views.T: Origen's commentary is lost, but Victorinus, Jerome (who follows Origen) and Chrysostom wrote full commentaries in the 300s. Augustine wrote on Galatians about AD 394-395. Luther lectured on it in 1516-17 (published 1519) and again in 1531 (published 1535), and and, in sayings recorded by others in his Table Talk, is reported to have called it the letter he was 'betrothed' to: 'my Katie von Bora'. The Reformers read 1:8-9 as a rule for testing every teaching, and Catholic teachers read it with 1:11-12 on the relation of Scripture and apostolic tradition.

deep.b:
The Gauls (Celts) crossed into Asia Minor in 278 BC and settled around Ancyra (now Ankara), Pessinus and Tavium. In 25 BC, when the last king, Amyntas, died, Augustus made Galatia a Roman province that took in not only the old Galatian homeland but also Pisidia, Lycaonia, Isauria and part of Phrygia. Pisidian Antioch and Lystra became Roman colonies. 'The churches of Galatia' (1:2; 1 Corinthians 16:1) can therefore mean either the northern region or the whole province.

North Galatian view (Lightfoot and most nineteenth-century commentators): the letter is to Celtic Galatians, evangelized on the second journey (Acts 16:6) or visited again on the third (Acts 18:23); it is written in the mid-50s, from Ephesus or Macedonia. Support: 'Galatians' in 3:1 reads naturally as an ethnic name; Acts 16:6 and 18:23 speak of 'the Phrygian and Galatian country'. South Galatian view (Ramsay, Bruce, Longenecker): Paul uses Roman provincial names elsewhere (Asia, Macedonia, Achaia, Syria), Acts 13-14 records churches in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe, and Barnabas, who was with Paul only on that first journey, is spoken of as known to the readers (2:1, 9, 13). Those who went with the collection to Jerusalem included Gaius of Derbe and Timothy, who came from Lystra (Acts 20:4; 16:1), which would fit the 'churches of Galatia' of 1 Corinthians 16:1.

The question matters for the date and for Acts: on the South Galatian view Galatians could be the earliest letter of Paul (late 40s), written before the Council of Acts 15, and the visit of 2:1-10 could be the famine visit of Acts 11:30. On the North view the letter is later and 2:1-10 is usually the Council. The letter's argument does not depend on the answer. The Plain follows neither view and keeps 'Galatians' and 'Galatia'.

deep.h: From the call to the meeting at Antioch: a timeline
deep.b:
Paul gives three time marks: three years (1:18), fourteen years (2:1) and the Antioch clash (2:11). Putting them beside Acts and the outside evidence gives a rough scheme, with dates that vary by a few years in the commentaries.

About AD 30 or 33: the death and resurrection of Jesus. About 31-36: Paul's call near Damascus (1:15-16; Acts 9). Then Arabia and Damascus; Paul escapes Damascus through a window under the governor of King Aretas IV (2 Corinthians 11:32-33), so before Aretas' death about AD 40. About 34-38: first Jerusalem visit, fifteen days with Cephas and James (1:18-19). Then Syria and Cilicia (1:21), about 36-45. About 43-45: Barnabas brings Paul to Antioch (Acts 11:25-26). About 46-49: the second visit to Jerusalem (2:1-10), the famine visit of Acts 11:30 or the Council of Acts 15. Then the clash at Antioch (2:11-14) and the writing of the letter, between about 48 and 57 depending on the view of Galatia and the visit.

The anchor for the later dates is the Gallio inscription at Delphi (Acts 18:12), which puts Paul in Corinth in about AD 51-52. Counting backward from there, Paul's call falls in the early to mid-30s.

deep.h: Who were the agitators, and how do we know?
deep.b:
Paul never describes the teachers who unsettled his churches, so everything we say about them is rebuilt from his answers. The method is called mirror-reading: if Paul denies something, someone may have asserted it. John Barclay's 1987 article warned that this is risky: Paul's replies may answer a charge nobody made, or a caricature.

The likeliest picture, from clues in the letter: they came to Galatia after Paul left (1:6-9; 4:16); they pressed Gentile believers to be circumcised and to keep the Sabbath and festival calendar (5:2-3; 4:10), probably by appeal to Genesis 17 and the covenant with Abraham, which Paul answers with the order of promise and law (3:15-18); they said, or were heard to say, that Paul had his gospel at second hand from Jerusalem (1:1, 11-12, 17) and that he was inconsistent (1:10; 5:11); and they were, Paul says, motivated by a wish to avoid persecution (6:12). They were not, on most readings, opposed to Christ; they thought the circumcised were the people of God and that the Gentiles must join them.

Views of their identity: Jewish Christians from Jerusalem (the 'Judaizers'); Gentile Christians who had adopted Jewish practice; or Jewish non-believers in the local synagogues who pressed the Gentile Christians to complete conversion (Nanos). The Plain uses Paul's own word 'some people who are upsetting you' and leaves their identity to the reader.

deep.h: The omitted thanksgiving and the form of the letter
deep.b:
A Greek letter normally had a greeting and a short wish for health. Paul's letters add a thanksgiving to God for the readers, which introduces the main theme (Romans 1:8-15; 1 Corinthians 1:4-9; Philippians 1:3-11). In Galatians it is missing. In its place stand the words 'I am amazed' (1:6) and a double curse (1:8-9). Betz argued that this is the signature of the 'rebuke letter', a genre in which the writer shows displeasure right at the start.

The shape that follows has been analyzed in two ways. Betz saw a speech for the defense: a statement of the facts (1:12-2:14), a proposition (2:15-21), proofs (3:1-4:31), an exhortation (5:1-6:10) and a close (6:11-18). Kennedy and others see a speech meant to persuade about the future, not to defend the past. Many scholars hold that Paul mixes the forms, since he was a letter-writer, not a rhetoric teacher. For readers, the point is that the letter is arranged as an argument aimed at a decision: do not be circumcised.

deep.title: Claude's theory: blessing and curse frame the letter
deep.b:
Galatians opens with a blessing (1:3, 'Grace to you and peace') and a curse (1:8-9, 'let him be accursed'), and it closes with another blessing (6:16, 'peace and mercy on them') and, at 6:17, a warning not to trouble Paul further. In between, Paul sets the curse of the law (3:10-13) against the blessing of Abraham (3:8-9, 14). These are the paired words of the covenant in Deuteronomy 27-30, where Israel hears blessings and curses read aloud and chooses between them. It may be that Paul has shaped the whole letter as a covenant renewal in which the Galatians are told, as Israel was told on the plains of Moab, to choose life or death (compare 5:1-6 and 6:7-8).

This overlaps with Betz's observation that Galatians has the formal curse and blessing of a covenant document, and with N. T. Wright's reading of Deuteronomy 27-30 behind 3:10-14. The new element, if there is one, is the suggestion that the letter as a whole is built around the choice, not only 3:10-14.

settings.by: Paul, with 'all the brothers who are with me' (1:2)
settings.to: The churches of Galatia, the churches Paul founded there (north or south, see the book introduction)
settings.when: Some years after Paul founded the churches, soon after the agitators had arrived (1:6)
settings.why: To claim an authority that does not come from people (1:1), to say who Jesus is (the one who gave himself 'for our sins', 1:4) and, by leaving out the usual thanksgiving, to tell the readers at the start that he is displeased. It prepares for the argument that follows.
settings.readers: Mostly Gentile believers who had left idols for the God of Israel (4:8), with some Jews. They knew Paul as their founder and would have noticed at once that the usual thanks were missing. The opening is read aloud in the assembly, and 'the churches' were meant to hear the letter together.
views: Celtic Galatians in the north, visited on the second and third journeys; letter written in the mid-50s.
Churches of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe (Acts 13-14); the letter may date from the late 40s.

settings.to: The Galatian churches; indirectly the agitators, whom he does not name
settings.when: At the point the news of the Galatians' change of loyalty had reached him
settings.why: To stop the change of loyalty by saying plainly what is at stake: there is only one good news, and anyone who changes it, whoever he is, is under a curse. He also meets the charge that he shapes his message to please people (1:10).
settings.readers: Gentile Christians who were being told that they needed circumcision to be full members of Abraham's family; the curse tells them that this is not a small question of detail.
views: The traditional view: teachers of the circumcision party who insisted that Gentile believers become proselytes.
Some of the Galatians themselves, drawn to the law, with no outside teachers needed.
Mark Nanos: 'influencers' who pressed Gentile followers of Christ to complete conversion.

settings.what: Paul's account of his call and his early years
settings.when: Told years after the events, in the letter
settings.why: To show that the good news he preached came from Jesus Christ by revelation and not from the Jerusalem apostles or from the church at Antioch, and that his later agreement with Jerusalem (2:1-10) was an agreement between equals. He is also answering a charge that he had received it from Jerusalem and then changed it (1:10).
settings.readers: The Galatians could not check the facts. They would have heard them as a witness's statement, sworn on oath (1:20), by the man who first gave them the good news.
views: Paul answers an accusation that he was a dependent of the Jerusalem apostles (Betz, Longenecker).
Paul uses his own story as an example of grace in action, not mainly as a defense (Dunn).

traditions.q: Who was 'James, the brother of the Lord'? (1:19)
views: 'Brother' is used broadly in the Old Testament for relatives; James and Joseph are sons of another Mary, so cousins of Jesus, and Mary remained a virgin all her life (Jerome, Against Helvidius, about AD 383; the Catechism, 500, speaks of the 'brothers' as 'close relations' of Jesus and does not name them cousins).

James and the other 'brothers' were sons of Joseph from an earlier marriage, stepbrothers of Jesus, and Mary is ever-virgin (Epiphanius, Panarion 78, late 300s). The Church keeps the feast of the Apostle James, the Lord's brother.
The Lutheran confessions call Mary 'ever virgin' (Smalcald Articles, Part 1), and Luther read 'brothers' as cousins or relatives; many Lutherans today leave the question open.

Calvin (Commentary on Galatians 1:19; on Matthew 13:55) took 'brothers' to mean kinsmen, as Jerome did, and rejected Helvidius's argument from Matthew 1:25 as unproved; later Reformed writers usually read the word in its plain sense, younger brothers born to Mary and Joseph.
No official teaching. Anglo-Catholics follow the Catholic or Eastern tradition; Evangelical Anglicans usually take the 'brothers' as younger siblings of Jesus.

Baptists have no doctrine of the perpetual virginity of Mary and usually take 'brother' in its plain sense: James was a younger brother of Jesus, born to Mary and Joseph (the view that Helvidius held).

title: At Jerusalem, at Antioch, and Crucified with Christ
sum: Fourteen years later Paul goes up to Jerusalem again with Barnabas and Titus and lays out before the leaders the good news he preaches to the Gentiles. The leaders add nothing. Titus, a Greek, is not made to be circumcised, in spite of 'false brothers' who sneaked in; James, Cephas and John give Paul and Barnabas their right hands, agreeing that Paul and Barnabas would go to the Gentiles, and they to the circumcised, with a request to remember the poor (2:1-10). Then at Antioch Paul opposes Cephas to his face when Cephas draws back from eating with Gentile believers (2:11-14).

The chapter ends with the heart of the letter. 'We know that a person is not justified by works of the law, except through faith in Jesus Christ' (2:16). Paul died to the law through the law; he has been crucified with Christ; and Christ lives in him. To return to the law as the way of righteousness would be to say that Christ died for no reason (2:15-21).
readings: The chapter reports a meeting with the Jerusalem leaders, an agreement, and a clash. It gives the earliest account of the meeting, written some years after it, and it complements Acts 15, though the two accounts differ and have to be set side by side.

Paul chooses what to tell in order to prove a case: that Jerusalem never required Gentiles to be circumcised, and that Cephas himself held the same view until fear moved him. The story of Antioch leads straight into the statement of the good news in 2:15-21, which is the proposition for the rest of the letter.
Read as a story of two ways to belong

The Jews of Antioch were choosing between two ways to belong to the people of God together at a meal: through Jewish practice, or through Christ alone. On this reading (Dunn, Wright) Paul's 'justification' language answers a question about table fellowship before it answers a question about private guilt.

views.H: The meeting at Jerusalem (2:1-10) is dated to the late 40s, and the leaders are James, Cephas and John. The Antioch church was a mixed community of Jews and Gentiles in the third city of the empire. Eating together was the daily test of belonging, and Jewish rules about food, wine from Gentiles and contact with idols made mixed meals a problem. Jerusalem in the 40s was under pressure from zealous Jews (Jewett), which may explain James' caution.
views.C: Whether 2:1-10 is the same event as Acts 15 or as the famine visit of Acts 11:30 is a main question for dating Paul and Galatians. The variant at 2:5 (a Western omission of 'not') is a famous case. The pistis Christou phrase of 2:16 and 2:20 is the main grammatical crux: faith in Christ, or the faithfulness of Christ. The quotation marks of 2:14-21 are modern; the Greek does not say where Paul's speech to Cephas ends.
views.L: Chapter 2 has three scenes: Jerusalem (2:1-10), Antioch (2:11-14) and Paul's statement of the gospel (2:15-21). Paul's sentences in 2:3-6 break off and start again, as if his emotions break the grammar. The words 'justified', 'works of the law' and 'faith' cluster in 2:16, then the 'I' takes over in 2:18-21. The crucifixion language of 2:19-20 is the center of the letter.
views.J: The Jew-Gentile division is the whole subject: 'the uncircumcised' and 'the circumcised' (2:7-9), 'Jews by nature' and 'Gentile sinners' (2:15), and the question whether a Gentile must 'judaize' (2:14). The New Perspective (Dunn, Wright) and Paul-within-Judaism scholars (Nanos, Gager) read it as an argument about Gentiles joining God's people without becoming Jews; the older Protestant reading also hears an argument about doing good works to be saved.
views.T: Origen and Chrysostom took the Antioch quarrel as a staged dispute between friends; Jerome followed them; Augustine said the rebuke was real. Luther's 1535 lectures on 2:16 made justification by faith alone the chief article of the church. Catholic teaching (Trent, session 6) denies that works done without grace justify and affirms the renewal of the believer; the Orthodox read 2:20 as union with Christ; the 1999 Joint Declaration states what Lutherans and Catholics now agree on.

deep.h: Jerusalem in Galatians 2 and in Acts
deep.b:
Paul and Acts both tell of a meeting between Paul and Barnabas and the Jerusalem leaders about Gentiles and circumcision. The accounts agree on the core: Paul and Barnabas went up to Jerusalem (Acts has them come from Antioch; Paul does not say from where); James, Peter (and John, in Paul) were there; the issue was circumcision of Gentile believers; the leaders did not require it. They differ in tone and detail. Paul describes a private meeting 'in answer to a revelation', with Titus in the company, 'false brothers' sneaking in, and the leaders adding nothing but a request to remember the poor (2:1-10). Acts 15 tells of a public gathering of apostles and elders, sent by the Antioch church after some from Judea taught that circumcision was necessary for salvation (Acts 15:1-2), with speeches by Peter and James and a letter to the Gentile believers asking them to keep away from "food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled and from sexual sin" (Acts 15:29). Paul never mentions the letter.

Views. (1) Galatians 2:1-10 is the Council of Acts 15 as Paul remembers it, and Galatians was written afterward; Acts has shaped its version (Lightfoot, Betz). (2) Galatians 2:1-10 is the famine visit of Acts 11:30 and 12:25; Acts 15 came later; Galatians was written before the Council, which explains why Paul never cites its letter (Ramsay, Bruce, Longenecker; the South Galatian view). The request to remember the poor fits the famine relief. (3) Acts 11:30 and Acts 15 are Luke's two tellings of one Jerusalem visit, so that Acts has three visits where Paul has two; Galatians 2:1-10 is Paul's own account of that one visit, and Paul's letter is the earlier and better witness where it differs from Acts (Haenchen, Lüdemann). These are not tied in bundles: some scholars combine a South Galatian address with the Council, and the view that Galatians 2 is the Council can go with a date in the late 40s or the mid-50s. Each view has difficulties. On (1), why does Paul say nothing of the decree? On (2), why does Acts not mention a clash over circumcision at the famine visit? On (3), why would Luke have told one visit twice?

Paul gives one side. Cephas had been eating with the Gentile believers at Antioch, as he had at Caesarea in the house of Cornelius (Acts 10:28; 11:3). When people 'from James' arrived, he drew back, and the other Jewish believers, even Barnabas, followed. Paul calls the behavior of Cephas and the others 'hypocrisy' (2:13), and says he told Cephas, in front of them all, that they 'were not walking straight toward the truth of the good news' (2:14).

What was at stake? Eating with Gentiles did not break the Torah by itself, but it raised problems in practice: whether the food had been prepared by Jewish rules, whether wine or meat had been offered to idols, and whether Gentiles were ritually unclean. Views: Dunn reads it as a dispute over Jewish food laws and purity as boundary markers; Nanos and Fredriksen see the weight on idolatry and on the Gentiles' standing, and say that Paul would not have thought Jewish believers ate un-kosher food; Esler stresses that the table was the place where social identity was made. In every view, withdrawal meant that Gentile believers had to choose to judaize or stay apart (2:14).

How did it end? Paul does not say. Dunn has argued that Paul lost the argument, since Barnabas and the Jewish Christians stayed with Cephas, and Acts 15:36-40 shows Paul parting from Barnabas and leaving Antioch. Others reply that Paul mentions Cephas and Barnabas as colleagues afterward (1 Corinthians 1:12; 9:5-6), and that Paul's silence is rhetorical: the Galatians knew how it came out. The incident had a long afterlife; see the card at 2:11-14 and the note on Jerome and Augustine below.

deep.h: 'Works of the law' and justification in 2:16
deep.b:
Verse 16 packs the letter's thesis into three clauses: no one is justified by works of the law; we have believed in Christ so that we may be justified by faith in Christ; and by works of the law no flesh will be justified. Almost every word is debated.

Works of the law. The older Protestant reading (Luther, Calvin) takes the phrase to mean any deed done to meet the law's demands, and Paul's argument to be against trying to earn righteousness. In 1977 E. P. Sanders argued that the Judaism of Paul's day taught that Israel was chosen by grace and that obedience was the response (he called it 'covenantal nomism'); many scholars have accepted this picture, though it is contested (Stephen Westerholm is a main critic, and the essays in Justification and Variegated Nomism test it text by text). James Dunn and N. T. Wright concluded that Paul's target is the practices, circumcision, food laws and the Sabbath, that marked Jews as God's people, which the Gentiles were being pressed to take on. Moo, Schreiner and others reply that 3:10 ('everyone who does not stay with all the things written') shows Paul has the whole law and its demand in view. The Dead Sea text 4QMMT, 'Some of the Works of the Torah', shows that the Hebrew phrase could refer to specific rules a sect judged necessary for the covenant community; it does not decide between the readings. A common middle position holds that Paul means both: the practices that divided Jews from Gentiles, as an example of the law in its whole demand.

Justified. The word is a law-court term in the Greek Bible, and the question is whether Paul means 'declare to be in the right', 'make righteous' or 'declare to belong to God's family'. Protestants have stressed the first, Catholics have included the second, and the New Perspective stresses the third. Each church's teaching is set out in the card.

Where consensus holds. Scholars agree that 2:16 is about Jew and Gentile on the one hand and about the way a person is right with God on the other, and that Paul sets 'works of the law' against faith in Christ. They differ on what the phrase excludes and on what justification means.

deep.h: Faith in Christ or the faithfulness of Christ?
deep.b:
Paul writes pistis Iesou Christou in 2:16 and 3:22, pistis Christou in 2:16 (second use), and 'the faith of the Son of God' in 2:20, 'faith in Christ Jesus' in 3:26 (with en). The Greek genitive 'of Christ' can name the object of faith ('faith in Christ', the objective genitive) or the one who has faith or is faithful ('Christ's faith' or 'faithfulness', the subjective genitive). The KJV's 'faith of Jesus Christ' preserves the ambiguity; most modern versions choose 'faith in'. Since Richard Hays's 1983 study and George Howard's 1967 article, many scholars have argued for the subjective reading.

For 'faith in Christ': the next clause of 2:16, 'we also believed in Christ Jesus', reads as the sum of the thought; the verb 'believe' in Paul often has Christ as its object; the Greek Fathers in general, and Luther and Calvin, took the genitive as objective. For 'the faithfulness of Christ': the genitive after pistis is subjective in 'the faith of Abraham' (Romans 4:12, 16) and 'the faithfulness of God' (Romans 3:3); the reading avoids the repetition ('through faith in Christ... we believed in Christ... by faith in Christ'); and it gives Christ's own obedience (Philippians 2:8; Romans 5:19) a place in justification. Dunn, Moo, Fitzmyer and Schreiner defend the first; Hays, Campbell, Longenecker (in the commentary) and Martyn the second; Wright, in part, accepts the second. Some call for a middle position: Paul speaks of Christ's faithfulness as the ground and of human trust as the response.

The Plain follows the objective reading, as it does in Romans 3:22 and 3:26, because of the clause in 2:16 that follows. It records the other reading in the variants at 2:16 and 3:22. The difference does not change Paul's main point that justification is by Christ and not by works of the law; it changes how much weight falls on the believer's act of faith.

Origen, in a commentary now lost, held that Paul only appeared to rebuke Peter, that the two had agreed to act out a quarrel so that the Gentile believers would hear that they did not need the law. Jerome took this over in his own commentary on Galatians (about AD 386-387), and John Chrysostom, in a homily on this passage, taught a similar view. Their motive was to protect the apostles' character: they could not suppose that Peter had been in the wrong or that Paul had been rude, or lied.

Augustine wrote about this to Jerome from 394 or 395 (Letter 28, which went astray and did not reach Jerome in that form) and again in Letter 40 (about 397), saying that this made Scripture itself a place where a 'useful lie' was permitted, which would destroy its authority. Peter had been wrong, and Paul had been right to say so, and Peter's humility in being corrected is an example to the church. Jerome replied in Letters 56 and 67 (about 402) and, in Letter 112, defended himself by saying that he followed Origen and other Greek commentators; the two exchanged several letters over about a decade, and Augustine's view has been the commoner one in the West since. Aquinas follows Augustine; Luther and Calvin make the incident a main plank against papal claims to infallibility. Catholics reply that infallibility attaches to teaching, not to every act of Peter's life.

echoes: Acts 10:28; Acts 11:3; Acts 15:1-35; Acts 16:3; Acts 21:20-24; Romans 3:20-31; Romans 6:3-11; Romans 7:4-6; Philippians 3:9; 1 Corinthians 9:5-6; Psalm 143:2; Genesis 17:10-14; Isaiah 53:12

settings.what: The meeting with the Jerusalem leaders
settings.by: Paul tells the story; the speakers in it are Paul, Barnabas, James, Cephas and John
settings.to: The Galatian churches, to whom Paul tells the story; in the story, the leaders of the Jerusalem church
settings.when: Fourteen years after (his call, or his first visit); about AD 46-50
settings.why: To show that the Jerusalem leaders, whom the agitators may have named as their authority, had not required circumcision of a Gentile believer and had added nothing to Paul's good news. It sets up the contrast with the Antioch incident and answers any suggestion that Paul's message was under Jerusalem's control.
settings.readers: Gentile Christians who had been told by the agitators that Jerusalem backed circumcision. Paul says that Jerusalem did not.
views: The meeting is the Council; Galatians was written afterward (Lightfoot, Betz).
The meeting is the visit with relief for the poor; Galatians was written before the Council (Ramsay, Bruce, Longenecker).
Acts 11:30 and Acts 15 are Luke's two tellings of one Jerusalem visit, which Galatians 2:1-10 remembers in Paul's own way (Haenchen, Lüdemann).

settings.what: Paul's opposition to Cephas at Antioch
settings.to: Cephas, with 'them all', the church at Antioch, Jews and Gentiles; heard again by the Galatians in the letter
settings.when: After the Jerusalem meeting, or before the Council of Acts 15, at Antioch
settings.why: To show that the 'truth of the good news' has to shape daily life, at table with Gentiles, and that even the first apostle can be wrong. It is a story about conduct that leads straight into the argument about justification.
settings.readers: The Galatians faced the same pressure from outside to treat Gentile believers as second-class. Paul tells them that Cephas himself gave in to fear and was challenged.
views: The incident came first and helped bring about the Council.
The clash took place when the agreement was already made, and shows how fragile it was (Lightfoot, Dunn).

settings.what: Paul's statement of the good news
settings.by: Paul, continuing his speech to Cephas or turning to the Galatians
settings.to: Cephas and the Jewish believers at Antioch, and the Galatians who are reading
settings.when: At Antioch, or Paul's later summary of what he said
settings.why: To lay down the doctrine that grounds his rebuke: no one is justified by works of the law, but by faith in Christ, and a believer who rebuilds the law as a wall makes Christ's death pointless. It is the proposition that the rest of the letter proves from the Galatians' experience (3:1-5), from Abraham (3:6-29) and from the Spirit (4:1-6:10).
settings.readers: Gentile believers who were being told to take on circumcision. The 'we' of 2:15-17 is Jewish believers; the 'I' of 2:18-21 is Paul speaking for himself and, by example, for them.
views: All of 2:15-21 is what Paul said at Antioch.
Verses 15-21 are Paul's own comment on the Antioch story, addressed to the Galatians.

traditions.q: What does the clash at Antioch show about Peter, and was it real? (2:11-14)
views: Peter's fault was a fault of conduct, not of teaching: infallibility does not mean sinlessness (Pastor Aeternus, ch. 4). Catholic teachers have been divided on whether the quarrel was real: Jerome, following Origen, thought it staged, and Augustine said it was real, and both are Doctors of the Church. Aquinas follows Augustine and holds that a subordinate may correct a superior publicly when the faith is in danger (Summa II-II, q. 33, a. 4).
Chrysostom taught that Peter and Paul acted out the quarrel for the sake of the Gentiles, as Origen had before him (Jerome in the West followed them); Orthodox writers do not all agree on this.

Luther: Peter erred in conduct, not in doctrine, and Paul rebukes him to defend the article of justification; the example shows that even great apostles can fall, and it is a warning to those who claim that the church cannot err.
Calvin: Peter's fault was real, and the story shows that Peter was not exempt from error, which overturns any claim that his successors cannot err.

Churches and councils can err (Article 19: 'the Church of Rome hath erred, not only in their living and manner of ceremonies, but also in matters of faith'). The Articles do not themselves mention Antioch.

traditions.q: What does 'justified... by faith in Christ and not by works of the law' mean, and how do faith and works relate? (2:16)
views: No one is justified by works done by natural strength or by the law apart from grace; faith is the beginning, foundation and root of justification, and justification includes the renewal of the inner person, with good works that flow from grace (Council of Trent, session 6; Catechism 1987-1995). The 1999 Joint Declaration, signed with the Lutheran World Federation, affirms that we are accepted by God 'by grace alone'.

The Fathers read 'faith working through love' (5:6) with 2:16: faith and works are two sides of one life in Christ, and justification is not separated from renewal and union with God. The Confession of Dositheus (1672) denies that faith alone justifies.

God declares the sinner righteous for Christ's sake, by faith alone, apart from works of the law (Augsburg Confession, art. 4). Luther called this the chief article of the faith (Smalcald Articles, Part 2, art. 1), and later Lutherans said it is the article by which the church stands or falls; Luther treated it most fully in his lectures on Galatians.

'Works of the law' means all works done to earn favor; God pardons and accepts the sinner for the sake of Christ's obedience, imputed and received by faith alone (Westminster Confession 11; Calvin, Institutes 3.11).

Justification is God's free pardon, received by faith alone; sanctification, the new birth and holiness follow, and faith 'works by love' (Wesley's Notes on Galatians 5:6 and his sermon 'Justification by Faith').

Justification is God's gracious and full acquittal of all who believe, on the ground of Christ's obedience and not of anything done by the sinner (Second London Confession 11; Baptist Faith and Message, 2000, art. 4).

'We are accounted righteous before God, only for the merit of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ, by faith' (Article 11); good works are the fruit of faith (Article 12). Anglicans include Evangelicals who stress the forensic reading and Anglo-Catholics who stress sacraments and growth.

title: Abraham's Children by Faith
sum: Paul turns from his story to the Galatians' own experience. 'You senseless Galatians! Who has put a spell on you?' Did they receive the Spirit by works of the law or by the hearing of faith (3:1-5)? Then he goes to Scripture. Abraham 'believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness', so those who are from faith are Abraham's sons; the Scripture told Abraham the good news ahead of time that all the nations would be blessed in him (3:6-9). Those who rely on works of the law are under a curse; Christ bought us free by becoming a curse for us, so that Abraham's blessing might reach the Gentiles and we might receive the promised Spirit (3:10-14).

The promise came 430 years before the law and the law cannot cancel it (3:15-18). The law was added on account of transgressions, until the offspring came, and acted like the attendant of a minor, locking us up until faith came (3:19-25). Now all who are baptized into Christ are sons of God, and the chapter reaches its summit: 'There is no Jew and no Greek. There is no slave and no free person. There is no male and female. For all of you are one in Christ Jesus' (3:26-29).
readings: Read as a story of two covenants in time

Paul sets out a timeline: promise (about 2000 BC), law (430 years later), Christ. The promise is first and cannot be canceled; the law is a temporary arrangement; faith 'comes' with Christ. The reading is history-of-salvation (Wright, Dunn) and stresses that the law has a legitimate but limited place.
Read as the contrast of law and promise

In the older Protestant reading (Luther, Calvin) the chapter is about two ways of relating to God: doing and receiving. The law shows sin and drives people to Christ; the promise is received by faith alone. The curse (3:10-13) falls on everyone who tries the first way.

J. Louis Martyn reads the chapter as the story of what God has done: the 'faith' that comes (3:23, 25) is Christ himself, God's act that ends the old order's rule. The chapter then belongs with 1:4 and 4:4-5 as proclamation of what has happened, not instruction about how to be saved.

views.H: The Galatians were former pagans (4:8) who had received the Spirit with signs (3:2-5). On the South Galatian view, Acts 13-14 records miracles and a stoning in this region. The Greek and Roman reader knew the paidagogos, the slave who took a boy to school (3:24), and the law of wills (3:15). The Roman world was full of slaves (3:28). The 'angels' of 3:19 reflect Jewish tradition about Sinai.
views.C: Textual points: 3:1 (the Byzantine addition 'that you should not obey the truth'); 3:12 (the added 'man'); 3:14 ('promise' or 'blessing', with Papyrus 46 for 'blessing'); 3:17 ('in Christ'); 3:22 (pistis Iesou Christou, a question of reading and not of manuscripts). The grammar of 3:22 (pistis Iesou Christou) and the unusually short 3:20 ('a mediator is not of one'; hundreds of readings) are the main puzzles. Paul's Old Testament quotations (Genesis 12:3; 15:6; Deuteronomy 27:26; 21:23; Habakkuk 2:4; Leviticus 18:5) follow the Greek version, with adjustments. The 'baptismal formula' of 3:26-28 may be older than Paul (Meeks).
views.L: The chapter is built from a chain of arguments: experience (3:1-5), Scripture (3:6-14), an everyday example (3:15-18), the law's purpose (3:19-25) and a declaration (3:26-29). Words that run through it: 'faith', 'promise', 'law', 'offspring', 'one' (3:16, 20, 28) and 'all' (3:22, 26, 28). The movement from 'under a curse' to 'blessing' to 'one' is a rise from threat to promise. Paul's questions (3:1-5, 19, 21) bring the Galatians into the argument.
views.J: Paul reads Abraham in a way that bypasses circumcision, the sign of the covenant in Genesis 17, which many Jews took as the mark of Abraham's family. Jewish traditions pictured Abraham as keeping the whole Torah before it was given (Mishnah Kiddushin 4:14). Paul's 'the law is not from faith' (3:12) and 'the curse of the law' (3:10) are disputed: for the New Perspective and the Paul-within-Judaism scholars (Wright, Nanos, Gager), they are about Israel's and the nations' place in the covenant; Jewish readers have noted how the chapter has been heard against Jews.
views.T: Origen, Chrysostom and Augustine all read 3:24 with the Pauline picture of law as preparation. Luther's 1535 lectures on 3:13 ('Christ... became a curse') develop his teaching that Christ takes on the sinner's guilt and the believer receives his righteousness. Calvin's three uses of the law draw on 3:19-24. In the Orthodox baptismal rite Galatians 3:27 ('As many as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ') is sung in place of the Trisagion on baptismal feasts, and the epistle read at baptism is Romans 6:3-11. Catholic teaching on the Old Law as a 'pedagogue' (Catechism 1963) builds on 3:24.

deep.h: Abraham in Galatians 3 and in Romans 4
deep.b:
Both letters argue from Genesis 15:6, 'Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness', and both press the order of events. Romans 4:9-12 points out that this was said before Abraham was circumcised (Genesis 17), so that he can be the father of the uncircumcised who believe as well as of the circumcised. Galatians 3:17 points out that the promise came 430 years before the law, so that the law cannot cancel it. Galatians adds Genesis 12:3 (the nations will be blessed in Abraham, 3:8), which shows that the good news to Gentiles was in the story from the beginning. Romans adds Genesis 17:5 (father of many nations, Romans 4:17) and 15:5 (so will your offspring be, Romans 4:18).

Galatians is silent about Genesis 17 and circumcision. That silence is probably the key to the situation in Galatia. The agitators, on the mirror-reading, appealed to Genesis 17:9-14: the covenant with Abraham requires circumcision, and the uncircumcised male 'will be cut off from his people'. Paul goes around this text, and goes back to chapters 12 and 15, where nothing is said of circumcision.

Jewish tradition stresses Abraham's obedience as well as his trust. Sirach 44:19-21 says Abraham 'kept the law of the Most High' and was found faithful in testing; 1 Maccabees 2:52 joins his faithfulness in testing to Genesis 15:6; Jubilees pictures him keeping the festivals before Sinai; and the Mishnah (Kiddushin 4:14) says that Abraham observed the whole Torah before it was given. Paul reads Genesis in the other direction: trust, not obedience, is what God counted, and it came first. Scholars of the New Perspective note that Paul's argument is a response to the Torah-centered view of Abraham, not to a belief that deeds could earn God's favor.

deep.h: The curse of the law and the cross (3:10-14)
deep.b:
These five verses hold the letter's darkest and boldest argument. Paul quotes four texts in a row: Deuteronomy 27:26 ('Cursed is everyone who does not stay with all the things written...'), Habakkuk 2:4 ('The righteous will live by faith'), Leviticus 18:5 ('The one who does them will live by them') and Deuteronomy 21:23 ('Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree'). Two of them pronounce a curse and the other two a promise of life; Paul sets them against each other, and Christ stands in the gap.

The first step, from 'cursed is everyone who does not stay with all the things written' to 'all who are from works of the law are under a curse', is not explained. Luther and Calvin supplied: no one stays with everything, so all who try are cursed. N. T. Wright and others supply: Deuteronomy 27-30 ends with exile as the curse on a covenant-breaking Israel, and the exile has not ended; so Israel as a people is under the curse, and Christ takes it on himself as Israel's representative so that the blessing of Abraham can reach the nations. Dunn: those who treat the law as the boundary marker of the covenant fall under its curse. Each reading has to explain why Paul does not say more.

The second step, that Christ became a curse by hanging on a tree, uses a text about the body of an executed criminal. For first-century Jewish readers, a crucified Messiah was a scandal (1 Corinthians 1:23; Justin, Dialogue 89-90); Paul himself may once have said so as a persecutor. He turns the scandal into good news. What the churches say about how the curse is borne is set out in the card.

Jewish readers note that the law itself provides for failure, through sacrifice and repentance, and that Deuteronomy 30 promises restoration. Paul's argument has to be read as an argument about the Messiah and the nations, not as a claim about what the Torah teaches about forgiveness.

Paul's argument that 'offspring' in the promise is singular and means Christ has been called brilliant and misleading. The Hebrew zera and the Greek sperma are collective singulars, like 'offspring', and the grammar does not exclude many. Paul notices the singular and uses it. The readers of his time were used to close readings of Scripture: the rabbis too drew arguments from the number of a noun. But the argument surprises, because the promises to Abraham obviously refer to many descendants (Genesis 15:5; 22:17).

Defenses: (1) The singular names the one who sums up the family, as the king stands for the people; Christ is the Davidic Messiah and so is the offspring (2 Samuel 7:12-14). (2) The singular is the 'one' who gathers the many, which is why 3:29 can say that those who belong to Christ are Abraham's 'offspring' (Wright). (3) Paul is making a point in the manner of his time and does not intend a literal-grammatical proof. Critics, Jewish and Christian, find the argument strained; defenders say it is not the base of Paul's case but an illustration. In all views, the passage ends with verse 29 and the 'many' belonging to the 'one'.

deep.h: Why the law, and for whom? (3:19-25)
deep.b:
Verse 19 asks the question every Jewish reader of Paul would ask: 'Why, then, the law?' Paul's answer is that the law was added on account of transgressions, until the offspring came; it was arranged by angels through a mediator; and it was an attendant for those 'under sin' until faith came. Every phrase is difficult, but the direction is clear: the law is temporary, and second to the promise.

Jewish tradition spoke very differently of Torah. The Wisdom of Ben Sira and the book of Baruch identify the law with God's wisdom (Sirach 24:23; Baruch 4:1), and the Mishnah teaches that Israel was given 'a precious instrument' (Avot 3:14). Paul does not deny the law's holiness (Romans 7:12) but denies it the power to give life (3:21) and the permanent role in the family of Abraham. Readers differ on whether he meant this for Gentiles only, who were never under it (Gager, Eisenbaum; see Nanos), or for Jews as well, whose life 'under the law' was now at an end (the traditional view; 4:4-5).

The 'we' of 3:23-25 matters. If it means Jews, the passage describes what the law was for Israel. If it means everyone, as the Reformers read it, then the law is the same attendant for the whole human race. The churches' teaching on the 'uses' of the law is set out in the card.

deep.h: Neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female (3:26-29)
deep.b:
Verses 26-28 look like a formula Paul has received: baptism into Christ, putting on Christ, and three pairs that no longer divide. Wayne Meeks suggested that this was an early baptismal declaration, and that the first part, about being 'one', also lies behind 1 Corinthians 12:13 and Colossians 3:11. In 3:28 the third pair changes its grammar, from 'neither... nor' to 'male and female', in the wording of Genesis 1:27: Paul hears creation in it.

A rabbinic blessing has a man thank God each day for not making him a Gentile, a woman or an ignoramus (Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 43b; 'slave' appears in the discussion there and in the Tosefta and Jerusalem Talmud forms). These sources are later than Paul, and whether an earlier custom lies behind them is uncertain. A Greek saying attributed to Thales (Diogenes Laertius 1.33) thanks fortune for being a human and not a beast, a man and not a woman, a Greek and not a barbarian. Many have read Paul's three pairs as a direct answer to a prayer like that. Whether Paul was thinking of it is uncertain.

What the verse means has been argued ever since. On the first pair, Daniel Boyarin sees Paul wanting to dissolve difference into a universal humanity; Nanos, Gager and Eisenbaum reply that Paul writes of Gentiles joining Israel's God as Gentiles, and does not erase the Jewish people. On the second, Paul does not call for abolishing slavery in this letter (1 Corinthians 7:21-24; Philemon), but the verse helped, many centuries later, to ground the case of those who did. On the third, churches differ on whether it opens all offices to women or speaks of equal standing and salvation in Christ while distinguishing roles. The cards set out the answers.

All agree that the verse puts every member of the church in the same standing before God, and that it goes on to claim that they are 'heirs according to the promise' (3:29).

deep.title: Claude's theory: three 'ones' and a mediator who is not of one
deep.b:
Three times in this chapter the word 'one' carries weight: the promise is to 'one', the offspring that is Christ (3:16); 'a mediator is not of one, but God is one' (3:20); and 'you are all one in Christ Jesus' (3:28). It may be that Paul is answering the agitators' use of Genesis 17 with a single idea. The circumcision covenant divides the human race into two (circumcised and uncircumcised); God is one, and so his promise must have one family, defined by one offspring.

On this reading 3:20 ('a mediator is not of one') says that the law, which Moses mediated, belonged to a single nation, set over against the other nations; but God is one, and the One he promised is the single offspring who holds Jew and Gentile together. The reading overlaps with N. T. Wright's account of 3:20 in The Climax of the Covenant, which also sets the Shema (Deuteronomy 6:4) against the law's division of peoples, and with Romans 3:29-30. What this note adds is the thread through 3:16, 3:20 and 3:28.
deep.refs: Galatians 3:16; Galatians 3:20; Galatians 3:28; Deuteronomy 6:4; Romans 3:29-30; Genesis 17:9-14

echoes: Genesis 12:3; Genesis 15:6; Genesis 17:5; Genesis 18:18; Genesis 22:18; Exodus 12:40; Deuteronomy 21:22-23; Deuteronomy 27:26; Leviticus 18:5; Habakkuk 2:4; Isaiah 53:1; Joel 2:28; Romans 1:17; Romans 4:1-25; Romans 8:14-17; 1 Corinthians 12:13; Colossians 3:11; Hebrews 2:2; Acts 14:1-23

settings.what: The Galatians' own experience of the Spirit
settings.when: At the opening of the argument, in the letter
settings.why: To begin from what the Galatians cannot deny: they received the Spirit when they heard the good news and believed, before any circumcision. The agitators now claim that more is needed; Paul asks where the Spirit came from, and calls them senseless to forget it.
settings.readers: Gentile believers in an area where Paul and Barnabas had worked miracles and been persecuted (Acts 13-14, on the South Galatian view). They had known the Spirit, and Paul calls on that memory.
views: 'Did you suffer so much' means persecution (Acts 14:19; 1 Thessalonians 2:14).
'Suffer' here means 'experience' good and bad (some recent commentators).

settings.what: The argument from Abraham and from the curse of the law
settings.when: In the letter, after the appeal to experience
settings.why: To show from Scripture that Gentiles who trust are already Abraham's children (3:6-9) and that the law cannot be the route to blessing because it brings a curse (3:10-12), from which Christ has bought believers free (3:13-14). It answers the agitators' use of Genesis 17, which tied Abraham's family to circumcision.
settings.readers: Gentile Christians who were being told they could not be Abraham's family without circumcision. Paul says that the Scripture itself 'told the good news ahead of time' to Abraham for the nations.
views: The curse is the law's demand
No one keeps all the law; everyone who relies on it is cursed (Luther, Calvin, Schreiner).
The curse of Deuteronomy 27-30 lay on Israel as a people until Christ (Wright).
The curse is a misreading of the law
Those who use the law as a boundary badge fall under its curse (Dunn).

settings.what: The covenant illustration and the promise
settings.when: In the letter, as a homely example before the more difficult question of what the law is for
settings.why: To show that a promise that is ratified cannot be canceled by a later law, even God's law. The example of a ratified covenant or will is taken from daily life, to make the point plain, and the argument about the singular 'offspring' closes it.
settings.readers: Ordinary believers who knew how wills and agreements worked in their cities. Paul says he is speaking 'in human terms', and expects them to follow.
views: 'Diatheke' means the covenant with Abraham, the Old Testament sense.
A pun with 'will' in everyday Greek (Burton, Lightfoot).

settings.when: In the letter, in answer to the question 'Why, then, the law?'
settings.why: To show the law a real but limited place: added on account of transgressions, delivered at second hand, guarding until faith came. It meets the objection that Paul teaches the law against God's promise, and it gives the Galatians a reason to stop treating the law as the road to the inheritance.
settings.readers: Gentile believers who had not been under the law, and the Jewish believers in the churches who had. Paul says 'we', which can include them all or only Jews.
views: Jews were held under Torah until Christ; Gentiles were outside (Gager, Eisenbaum).
The law was an attendant for all humanity under sin (the Reformers).

settings.what: Sons of God, one in Christ
settings.by: Paul, perhaps quoting a baptismal declaration
settings.to: The Galatian churches, spoken to as 'you' in the second person plural
settings.when: At the high point of the argument, after the law's role is shown to be temporary
settings.why: To declare that those who are baptized into Christ are all sons of God and Abraham's offspring, without the distinctions that circumcision and the law marked: Jew and Greek, slave and free, male and female. It states positively what 3:1-25 argued negatively.
settings.readers: A church with Jews and Gentiles, slaves and free, men and women, being told to divide by circumcision. Paul says the baptism that joined them has already made them one.
views: A declaration made at baptism, known to the Galatians already (Meeks).
Paul writes it for this letter, echoing creation language.

traditions.q: How does Christ's death remove 'the curse of the law'? (3:10-14)
views: Christ's passion was a sacrifice and satisfaction offered out of love; he bore the punishment due to sin and merited grace for all (Aquinas, Summa III, qq. 46-48; Catechism 615-617).

Christ, by taking on the curse and death, destroyed death and freed humanity from corruption; the Church speaks of victory, ransom and healing and is cautious about penal substitution, which grew in the West (Chrysostom on Galatians 3:13).

Christ took on himself the sin of all and the law's curse in our place; in Luther's 1535 lectures he is made 'the greatest sinner' and the curse falls on him, so that believers are freed in a 'happy exchange'.
Christ bore the curse in the place of the elect as the penalty of the law (Calvin, Institutes 2.16.6; Heidelberg Catechism, Q. 39, on why the cross, a death cursed by God, was the means).
Christ's one oblation on the cross is the perfect redemption, propitiation and satisfaction for all sin (Article 31); Anglicans hold several theories of how.

traditions.q: What is the law for now that Christ has come? (3:19-25)
views: The law has two uses, to keep order and to show sin and drive people to Christ, which Luther made chief; the Formula of Concord adds a third use as a guide for the reborn, which some Lutherans dispute.
The law has three uses: to restrain, to convict and to guide believers, which Calvin calls its 'principal' use (Institutes 2.7; Westminster Confession 19).

The Old Law is holy, spiritual and good, yet imperfect: like an attendant (the Catechism's word is 'pedagogue') it shows what must be done but does not give the strength to do it. It is fulfilled in the New Law of the Gospel; the moral precepts remain, and the ceremonial and judicial precepts have passed (Catechism 1961-1964; Aquinas, Summa I-II, qq. 98-108).

The law was a preparation and a guide leading to Christ (Chrysostom on 3:24); the Church does not speak of 'uses' of the law but holds that Christians keep the commandments of Christ and the moral law.
Wesley: the moral law binds believers still; its first use is to convict, its second to bring to Christ, its third to keep believers alive to God.

Adventists distinguish the moral law, the Ten Commandments, which they hold remains binding (including the seventh-day Sabbath), from the ceremonial law of sacrifices, which they hold ended at the cross; many Adventist writers read the 'added' law and the 'attendant' of Galatians 3 as the ceremonial law, though Adventist interpreters have not all agreed on this (Fundamental Beliefs, 19).

The Mosaic covenant was a temporary arrangement for Israel, ended in Christ; the church is not under it, and its moral norms are restated in the New Testament (as in Ryrie's account of dispensations).

Jewish believers in Jesus remain Jews and may keep the Torah as an expression of covenant identity; Gentile believers are not bound by it. 'No longer under the attendant' (3:25) speaks of Gentiles' standing and of the law as a means of righteousness.

traditions.q: What does it mean to be 'baptized into Christ' and to 'put on Christ'? (3:27)
views: Baptism incorporates a person into Christ and the church and gives new life; the white garment given at baptism signifies that the person has 'put on Christ' (Catechism 1213, 1243).
Baptism is a participation in Christ's death and resurrection, followed at once by chrismation and the giving of a white robe; Galatians 3:27 is sung as the baptismal hymn on feast days.

Baptism is a means of grace in which God forgives sin and gives new birth (Small Catechism, part 4, on Baptism); in his 1535 lectures on Galatians 3:27 Luther reads 'put on Christ' of baptism and of the believer's clothing with Christ's righteousness.
Baptism is a sign and seal of union with Christ and of the covenant of grace; infants of believers are baptized (Westminster Confession 28).
Baptism by immersion is the believer's public picture of union with Christ; it follows faith and does not itself give union (Second London Confession 29).

traditions.q: Does 'no male and female' open every office in the church to women? (3:28)
views: Galatians 3:28 teaches the equal dignity of men and women in baptism and in grace; the church holds that she has no authority to ordain women to the priesthood (John Paul II, Ordinatio Sacerdotalis, 1994; Catechism 1577).
Men and women are equal in Christ, and many ministries are open to women; the priesthood is reserved to men according to the tradition of the church.

Divided: the ELCA and several other Lutheran churches ordain women, reading 3:28 together with the gifts of the Spirit; the Lutheran Church-Missouri Synod holds that the pastoral office is for men, citing 1 Corinthians 14:34 and 1 Timothy 2:12.

The Church of England has ordained women priests since 1994; legislation admitting women to the episcopate received final approval in November 2014, and the first woman bishop was consecrated in January 2015. Some Anglican provinces and many Anglo-Catholics do not accept this.

Reformed churches are divided: the Presbyterian Church in America limits the offices of elder and minister to men, while the Presbyterian Church (USA) has ordained women since 1956; each side cites 3:28 and the Pauline passages on teaching and authority differently.

The Methodist Church gave women full clergy rights in 1956, and the United Methodist Church ordains women as elders and bishops, reading 3:28 with the Spirit's gifts; some Methodist bodies outside it hold the pastoral office for men.
The Baptist Faith and Message (2000, art. 6) limits the office of pastor to men; other Baptist bodies ordain women and cite 3:28.
Many Pentecostal churches, including the Assemblies of God, ordain women, citing 3:28, Joel 2:28 (the Spirit on sons and daughters) and the Spirit's gifts.

traditions.q: What does 'no Jew and no Greek' mean for Jewish and Gentile believers? (3:28)
views: The church draws life from the root of the olive tree that is Israel; the Jews remain dear to God, whose gifts and calling are irrevocable, and the church does not replace them (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 839-840).

The fathers called the church the true or new Israel in which Jew and Greek are one in Christ (for example Justin, Dialogue 11 and 123), and Orthodox writers usually still speak this way, without teaching that God has cast off the Jews; ethnic privilege is not a ground of salvation.
The ELCA's 1994 Declaration to the Jewish Community rejects Luther's anti-Jewish writings and affirms respect for Jewish life; Lutheran teaching holds that Jew and Greek are one in Christ by faith.
There is one people of God under one covenant of grace; Jew and Gentile are one by faith. Reformed writers differ on whether Israel has a future as a nation.
Galatians 3:28 speaks of equal standing in salvation and does not abolish the distinction between Israel and the church or Israel's national promises (as in Ryrie).
Jewish believers remain Jews and Gentile believers remain Gentiles, one in Christ; Jewish believers may keep Torah as a covenant calling, and Gentile believers are not required to.
